plan: SAT R&W batch 76: 20 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000724..000743 (9 SEC: Katherine Dunham finite verb, Gertrude Ederle agreement and tense, Paul R. Williams plural vs possessive, Dolores Huerta past perfect, Ellen Ochoa modifier, Duke Kahanamoku however, Lonnie Johnson semicolon, Florence Price pronoun, Ruth Asawa paired dashes; jumping spider and Hansberry WIC; crow mask study sentence function; leafcutter ant purpose; Patricia Bath central idea; Bajau spleen inference; Venus flytrap quantitative evidence (student data); Jovita Idar inference; Bessie Stringfield and Arthur Ashe transitions; Noguchi Akari synthesis). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus S075-06 and S075-19 (revision 2) on previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A dancer's research
passages.text: Katherine Dunham, a dancer and anthropologist who had studied dance in Haiti and other Caribbean nations in the 1930s, ______ a dance company whose performances blended Caribbean traditions with ballet and modern dance.

passages.title: Across the Channel
passages.text: In 1926, Gertrude Ederle became the first woman to swim across the English Channel. Her time of 14 hours and 39 minutes, about two hours faster than that of any of the men who had made the crossing before her, ______ the women's record until 1950.

passages.title: An architect for the stars
passages.text: Paul R. Williams, who in 1923 became the first Black member of the American Institute of Architects, designed thousands of buildings in his career, including homes for many of Hollywood's best-known ______

passages.title: Before the union
passages.text: Dolores Huerta is best known as a labor leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with César Chávez in 1962. Before she helped start the union, Huerta ______ as an elementary school teacher, an experience that she later said showed her how poverty affected the children of farmworkers.

passages.title: A scientist in orbit
passages.text: Ellen Ochoa earned a doctorate in electrical engineering and helped develop optical systems for analyzing images before she joined the astronaut program. Selected by NASA in 1990, ______

passages.title: A champion of the waves
passages.text: Duke Kahanamoku of Hawaii won three Olympic gold medals in swimming, in 1912 and 1920. He is best remembered, ______ for spreading the sport of surfing, which he demonstrated to large crowds in Australia, the mainland United States, and elsewhere.

passages.title: An accidental invention
passages.text: In 1982, while working on a heat pump that used water instead of chemical coolants, engineer Lonnie Johnson attached a nozzle to his test device and sent a powerful stream of water across his ______ the moment gave him the idea for the Super Soaker, which went on to become one of the best-selling toys in the world.

passages.title: Lost music found
passages.text: In 1933, the Chicago Symphony Orchestra performed Florence Price's Symphony in E Minor, making Price the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra. Many of her manuscripts were long thought lost. In 2009, however, a couple renovating her former summer home in St. Anne, Illinois, found ______ in the attic.

passages.title: Sculptures of wire
passages.text: Ruth Asawa's best-known sculptures—hanging forms made of looped ______ seem to float in the air, and their shapes appear to change as a viewer walks around them.

passages.title: Seeing like a spider
passages.text: Most spiders rely on touch and vibration to find prey, but jumping spiders have remarkably ______ vision: their large front eyes let them judge distances precisely enough to leap onto insects several body lengths away.

passages.title: A first on Broadway
passages.text: When Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun opened in 1959, it became the first play by a Black woman to be produced on Broadway. The play's success was ______: it ran for more than 500 performances, and Hansberry became the youngest American playwright at that time to win the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award.

passages.title: Crows remember
passages.text: In a study at the University of Washington, researchers wearing a particular rubber mask trapped and banded several wild crows, then released them unharmed. In the years that followed, crows on campus scolded and mobbed anyone wearing that mask, even crows that had never been trapped. People wearing a different mask were mostly ignored. The researchers concluded that crows can recognize individual human faces and can learn from other crows which people to avoid.

passages.title: Farmers of fungus
passages.text: Leafcutter ants are often seen carrying pieces of leaves many times their own weight back to their nests. The ants do not eat the leaves. Instead, they chew them into a pulp that they use to grow a fungus in underground gardens, and the fungus, not the leaves, is the colony's main food. Some biologists describe leafcutter ants as among the earliest farmers on Earth, since they have been cultivating fungus for millions of years.

passages.title: A tool for the eye
passages.text: Ophthalmologist Patricia Bath invented the Laserphaco Probe, a device that uses a laser to break up cataracts so that they can be removed more precisely. When she received a patent for it in 1988, she became the first Black woman doctor in the United States to receive a patent for a medical invention. The probe has since helped restore sight to many patients around the world.

passages.title: Divers of the sea
passages.text: The Bajau people of Southeast Asia have lived largely at sea for generations, and many Bajau divers spend hours each day underwater, collecting food with little equipment. During a dive, the spleen contracts and releases oxygen-rich red blood cells into the bloodstream. A 2018 study found that Bajau people have spleens about 50 percent larger than those of a neighboring group that does not dive. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: A trap that counts
passages.text: A Venus flytrap's leaf snaps shut when an insect touches the small trigger hairs inside it. A student hypothesized that a trap closes only if a hair is touched twice within a short time, which would keep the plant from wasting energy on raindrops or debris. The student touched the hairs of 60 healthy traps: 20 were touched once, 20 were touched twice within 20 seconds, and 20 were touched twice 60 seconds apart. Of these, 0, 19, and 3 traps closed, respectively.

passages.title: A voice for her community
passages.text: Jovita Idar was a journalist in Laredo, Texas, who wrote for her family's Spanish-language newspaper, La Crónica, in the early 1900s. Her articles criticized discrimination against Mexican Americans and called for better schools for their children. In 1911, she helped found the League of Mexican Women, which offered free classes to poor children. For Idar, writing and organizing appear to have been closely connected.

passages.title: Riding alone
passages.text: In the 1930s, Bessie Stringfield rode a motorcycle across the United States by herself several times, at a time when few women of any background rode motorcycles. As a Black woman traveling through the segregated South, she was often refused lodging. ______ she sometimes slept on her motorcycle at gas stations.

passages.title: Two firsts
passages.text: Arthur Ashe won the first U.S. Open of the professional era in 1968, while he was still an amateur. ______ in 1975, he defeated the heavily favored Jimmy Connors to become the first Black man to win the singles title at Wimbledon.

passages.title: Notes on light
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Isamu Noguchi was a Japanese American sculptor and designer.
- In 1951, he began designing a series of lamps called Akari.
- The lamps were made of handmade paper stretched over thin bamboo frames.
- They were inspired by lanterns made in the Japanese city of Gifu.
- Noguchi designed more than 100 Akari lamps over several decades.

passages.title: A final journey
passages.text: Roberto Clemente spent eighteen seasons with the Pittsburgh Pirates and finished his career with exactly 3,000 hits. On December 31, 1972, he died in a plane crash while flying relief supplies to earthquake survivors in Nicaragua. Honored the following year in a special election, ______

passages.title: An empire of ants
passages.text: Where they have been introduced outside South America, Argentine ants from different nests usually treat one another as nestmates rather than as rivals, and they rarely fight. ______ in parts of southern Europe, connected nests of these ants form a single "supercolony" that stretches for roughly 6,000 kilometers along the coast.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: whose performances blended Caribbean traditions
candidates.explanation: The subject "Katherine Dunham" needs a main verb after the long appositive; "founded" supplies it.

A.rationale: "Founding" is not a main verb, so the sentence has no main verb for its subject.

B.rationale: "Having founded" is not a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

D.rationale: "Who" makes a second relative clause, leaving "Katherine Dunham" without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject, and does it have a main verb?

strategy.explanation: Skip the appositive between the commas.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a main verb for its subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Her time of 14 hours and 39 minutes
candidates.explanation: The singular subject "time" and the completed period ending in 1950 call for "remained."

B.rationale: "Remain" is plural and present, but the subject "time" is singular and the event is past.

C.rationale: "Have" is plural, and the present perfect does not fit a record that ended in 1950.

D.rationale: "Remaining" is not a main verb, so the sentence would lack one.

hints: What is the subject of the verb: the time or the men?

strategy.explanation: Skip the phrase between the commas.

candidates.remember: A verb agrees with its subject, not with a nearby noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: including homes for many of Hollywood's
candidates.explanation: "Many of Hollywood's best-known stars" needs a plain plural noun with no possession.

A.rationale: The singular possessive suggests one star owned something; the sentence needs a plain plural.

C.rationale: The plural possessive is wrong because nothing belongs to the stars in this sentence.

D.rationale: This is not a correct form of any word.

hints: Does anything belong to the stars here?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the noun is plural, possessive, or both.

candidates.remember: Plural nouns that show no possession take no apostrophe.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Before she helped start the union
candidates.explanation: Her teaching came before she helped start the union in 1962, so the past perfect "had worked" is correct.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action completed before another past event.

B.rationale: The present tense does not fit an action in the past.

C.rationale: The future perfect does not fit an action in the past.

hints: Which happened first: the teaching or the union?

strategy.explanation: Find the time signal in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past events.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the shuttle Discovery carried Ochoa into space in 1993, making her the first Hispanic woman in space.
choices.B: Ochoa's flight aboard the shuttle Discovery in 1993 made her the first Hispanic woman in space.
choices.C: Ochoa became the first Hispanic woman in space when she flew aboard the shuttle Discovery in 1993.
choices.D: a 1993 flight aboard the shuttle Discovery made Ochoa the first Hispanic woman to go into space.

candidates.evidence: Selected by NASA in 1990
candidates.explanation: The introductory phrase describes Ochoa, so her name must come right after the comma.

A.rationale: The shuttle was not selected by NASA in 1990; Ochoa was.

B.rationale: The phrase would describe Ochoa's flight, but the flight was not selected by NASA; Ochoa was.

D.rationale: The flight was not selected by NASA in 1990; Ochoa was.

hints: Who was selected by NASA in 1990?

strategy.explanation: Match the opening phrase to the noun after the comma.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: He is best remembered
candidates.explanation: "However" interrupts the clause "He is best remembered for spreading the sport," so it is set off by a pair of commas.

A.rationale: A semicolon after "however" would cut the sentence in the middle of a clause.

C.rationale: "However" interrupts the clause and must be set off by commas on both sides.

D.rationale: A colon cannot follow "however" in the middle of a clause.

hints: Is "however" joining two clauses or interrupting one?

strategy.explanation: Check whether the words before "however" form a complete sentence that ends there.

candidates.remember: Set off an interrupting "however" with commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the moment gave him the idea for the Super Soaker
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly joins them.

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from its clause.

hints: Can the words after the blank stand alone as a sentence?

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join independent clauses with a semicolon or a comma and conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Many of her manuscripts were long thought lost
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "manuscripts," which is plural, so "them" is correct.

B.rationale: "It" is singular, but it refers to the plural "manuscripts."

C.rationale: "This" is singular and has no clear antecedent.

hints: What did the couple find?

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the pronoun replaces.

candidates.remember: A pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: best-known sculptures—hanging forms
candidates.explanation: The phrase "hanging forms made of looped wire" interrupts the sentence after an opening dash, so a closing dash is needed.

A.rationale: A phrase opened with a dash must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot close a phrase opened with a dash.

D.rationale: Without a closing dash, the interrupting phrase runs into the verb.

hints: How does the interrupting phrase begin?

strategy.explanation: Find the punctuation that opens the phrase.

candidates.remember: Close an interrupting phrase with the same mark that opened it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: judge distances precisely enough to leap onto insects
candidates.explanation: Vision that allows precise distance judgments is sharp, or acute.

A.rationale: Judging distances precisely requires sharp, not blurry, vision.

B.rationale: Limited vision would not allow precise leaps.

C.rationale: The text contrasts these spiders with most others, so their vision is not ordinary.

hints: What does the explanation after the colon say the eyes can do?

strategy.explanation: Predict from the explanation after the colon.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after a colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it ran for more than 500 performances
candidates.explanation: A long run and a major award show that the play's success was considerable.

A.rationale: A long run and a major award show that the success was not in doubt.

C.rationale: More than 500 performances does not suggest brief success.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text suggests the success was expected.

hints: What evidence of success follows the colon?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word from the evidence after the colon.

candidates.remember: Use the explanation after a colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It shows that the crows reacted to one particular mask, not to masks in general.
choices.B: It explains why the researchers chose to wear masks rather than show their own faces.
choices.C: It introduces a finding that contradicts the conclusion stated at the end of the text.
choices.D: It describes how the crows were trapped and banded before being released unharmed.

candidates.evidence: People wearing a different mask were mostly ignored.
candidates.explanation: By noting that a different mask was ignored, the sentence shows the crows reacted to one specific mask, which supports face recognition.

B.rationale: The sentence reports the crows' reaction, not the reason for the masks.

C.rationale: The sentence supports the conclusion; it does not contradict it.

D.rationale: The trapping is described in the first sentence.

hints: What does the different mask let the researchers rule out?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the sentence adds to the argument.

candidates.remember: A comparison sentence often rules out an alternative explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To compare the strength of leafcutter ants with that of other ant species
choices.B: To argue that leafcutter ants were the first animals of any kind to live underground
choices.C: To describe how biologists first discovered the gardens of leafcutter ants
choices.D: To explain what leafcutter ants actually do with the leaves they collect

candidates.evidence: The ants do not eat the leaves
candidates.explanation: The text corrects a likely assumption by explaining that the ants use the leaves to grow fungus they eat.

A.rationale: No other ant species are discussed.

B.rationale: The text says nothing about the first underground animals.

C.rationale: The text does not describe a discovery.

hints: What surprising fact does the text reveal about the leaves?

strategy.explanation: Identify what most of the text explains.

candidates.remember: A main purpose must fit the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bath was the first doctor to discover that untreated cataracts could eventually cause blindness.
choices.B: Bath invented a laser tool for cataract surgery and earned a pioneering medical patent.
choices.C: Lasers have replaced every other method of eye surgery used by doctors since the 1980s.
choices.D: Bath received many patents for devices that are now used in several areas of medicine.

candidates.evidence: she became the first Black woman doctor in the United States to receive a patent
candidates.explanation: The text describes Bath's laser cataract device and the milestone of her 1988 patent.

A.rationale: The text does not say Bath discovered this.

C.rationale: The text makes no such broad claim.

D.rationale: The text mentions only one patent.

hints: What two things does the text say about Bath?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the text in one sentence before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: Bajau divers do not need their spleens to supply oxygen during their dives.
choices.B: the neighboring group dives more often than the Bajau do but for shorter periods.
choices.C: a larger spleen may help Bajau divers stay underwater longer by supplying more oxygen.
choices.D: the size of a person's spleen has no effect at all on how long that person can stay underwater.

candidates.evidence: releases oxygen-rich red blood cells into the bloodstream
candidates.explanation: If the spleen releases oxygen-rich blood during dives, a larger spleen could supply more oxygen and allow longer dives.

A.rationale: This contradicts the text's description of the spleen's role.

B.rationale: The text says the neighboring group does not dive.

D.rationale: This contradicts the link the text sets up between the spleen and oxygen.

hints: What does the spleen do during a dive?

strategy.explanation: Connect the spleen's role to the size difference.

candidates.remember: A logical completion must follow from the details given.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's hypothesis?

choices.A: Of traps touched twice within 20 seconds, 19 closed; of those touched 60 seconds apart, only 3 did.
choices.B: Of the 60 healthy traps in the experiment, a total of 22 closed after their trigger hairs were touched.
choices.C: None of the 20 traps that were touched only once closed during the student's experiment.
choices.D: The student divided the 60 healthy traps into three equal groups of 20 traps each.

candidates.evidence: Of these, 0, 19, and 3 traps closed
candidates.explanation: Only this choice compares two touches close together with two touches far apart, which tests the "short time" part of the hypothesis.

B.rationale: This total does not compare the timing of the touches.

C.rationale: This shows one touch is not enough but does not address how quickly the second touch must come.

D.rationale: This describes the design, not the results.

hints: Which part of the hypothesis depends on timing?

strategy.explanation: Match the data to every part of the claim.

candidates.remember: The best evidence addresses the specific claim.

candidates.stem: Based on the text, why did Idar most likely help found the League of Mexican Women?

choices.A: To gain readers for her family's newspaper among wealthy families in Laredo
choices.B: To replace her work as a journalist, which she had given up by 1911
choices.C: To protest a decision by her family to stop publishing in Spanish
choices.D: To act on concerns about education that she had also raised in her articles

candidates.evidence: called for better schools for their children
candidates.explanation: Her articles called for better schools, and the league offered free classes, so the league acted on the same concern.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the league was meant to attract readers.

B.rationale: The text does not say she gave up journalism and presents her writing and organizing as connected.

C.rationale: The text says nothing about such a decision.

hints: What did her articles call for, and what did the league offer?

strategy.explanation: Connect the league's work to her writing.

candidates.remember: An inference should link details the text actually gives.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: she was often refused lodging
candidates.explanation: Being refused lodging caused her to sleep on her motorcycle, so a cause-effect transition fits.

A.rationale: Sleeping on her motorcycle follows from being refused lodging; it does not contrast with it.

C.rationale: Sleeping on her motorcycle is a consequence, not a similar point.

D.rationale: The last sentence does not restate the previous one.

hints: How does sleeping at gas stations relate to being refused lodging?

strategy.explanation: Name the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Choose the transition that matches the logical relationship.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: in 1975, he defeated the heavily favored Jimmy Connors
candidates.explanation: The text moves from 1968 to 1975, so a time transition fits.

A.rationale: The Wimbledon win is not an example of the 1968 victory.

B.rationale: The two victories do not contrast; the second follows the first in time.

D.rationale: The 1968 win did not cause the 1975 win.

hints: How many years separate the two victories?

strategy.explanation: Use the dates to find the relationship.

candidates.remember: Choose the transition that matches the logical relationship.

candidates.stem: The student wants to describe the materials of Noguchi's Akari lamps. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Isamu Noguchi, a Japanese American sculptor, began designing his Akari lamps in 1951.
choices.B: Noguchi's Akari lamps were inspired by traditional lanterns from Gifu, Japan.
choices.C: Noguchi designed more than 100 Akari lamps over the course of several decades.
choices.D: Noguchi's Akari lamps were made of handmade paper stretched over thin bamboo frames.

candidates.evidence: handmade paper stretched over thin bamboo frames
candidates.explanation: Only this choice describes what the lamps were made of.

A.rationale: This gives the date, not the materials.

B.rationale: This gives the inspiration, not the materials.

C.rationale: This gives the number of designs, not the materials.

hints: Which note describes materials?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must meet the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the Baseball Hall of Fame inducted Clemente as its first Latin American player.
choices.B: Clemente's induction into the Baseball Hall of Fame made him its first Latin American player.
choices.C: a special election made Clemente the first Latin American player in the Baseball Hall of Fame.
choices.D: Clemente became the first Latin American player inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

candidates.evidence: he died in a plane crash
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes the person who was honored, so "Clemente" must come immediately after the comma.

A.rationale: The Hall of Fame was not honored; Clemente was.

B.rationale: The phrase "Honored the following year" would describe "Clemente's induction," but Clemente, not his induction, was honored.

C.rationale: The election was not honored; Clemente was.

hints: Who was honored?

strategy.explanation: Find the noun the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it describes.

revision_history.reason: blind solver A (nonblocking): in B the subject 'the first Latin American player...' refers to Clemente, so B was not a clear dangling-modifier error
revision_history.change: B rewritten so its subject is 'Clemente's induction', a clear dangling modifier; key and passage unchanged

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: they rarely fight
candidates.explanation: Because ants from different nests do not fight, their nests can link into a vast supercolony, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

A.rationale: The supercolony follows from the lack of fighting; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: The supercolony is consistent with the ants' cooperation, not opposed to it.

D.rationale: The supercolony is a consequence of the behavior, not a similar point.

hints: Is the supercolony a result of the ants' behavior?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before choosing.

candidates.remember: Use "As a result" for a consequence.

revision_history.reason: blind solver B (nonblocking, factual): passage stated without qualification that Argentine ants from different nests rarely fight; in the native range colonies are territorial
revision_history.change: passage now limits the claim to introduced populations ('Where they have been introduced outside South America'); items and key unchanged
